A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same manifold-denoising framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-manifold simulations and gravitational-wave denoising experiments, including training curves and numerical accuracy–complexity comparisons in Figures 8–9 and Table 1.

after.justification: v2 reports gravitational-wave experiments and adds original autoencoder comparisons, natural-image denoising experiments, and component ablations in Appendix G.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the online graph-learning and mixed-order traversal framework. However, Appendix D revises the stated tangent-space update: Algorithms 4–5 replace inputs x_i with landmark-centered inputs x_i - q_M and formulate the update through eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix. This is a localized revision to the documented procedure.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic manifolds and generated gravitational waveforms. v2 retains this coverage and adds patch denoising using 300 ImageNet images and a single DIV2K image (Appendices G.2–G.3), substantially extending the domain and introducing a single-image learning scenario.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative comparison uses nearest-neighbor search. v2 retains it and adds 15 autoencoder configurations (Figure 13, Table 2), plus first-order-only traversal and zero-order search over all graph edges (Figure 18). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The gravitational-wave test set increases from 5,000 to 20,000 samples, while training remains at 100,000. New image protocols use 8 × 8 × 3 patches, Gaussian noise with sigma 0.1, and 890,000 or 170,000 training patches with strides 8 or 4. v2 also introduces autoencoder configurations and controlled component-ablation procedures. The retained hyperparameter table relabels the neighbor-radius entries from R_nbrs to R_nbrs squared.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained radius comparison and network visualizations, Appendix G.4 adds a controlled ablation testing why gradient steps and zero-order tunnels should be combined. Appendix B.2 adds a noisy-versus-denoised waveform case, and G.2–G.3 provide image and patch case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The larger test set changes evaluation size, while the theoretical probability bounds concern mathematical guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 8–9 show revised gravitational-wave curves, with Figure 9 using the enlarged test set. v1 Table 1's exact landmark counts, computational costs, and MSEs are removed. v2 adds autoencoder outcomes, image-denoising curves and examples, and ablation findings showing low computational cost but high error for first-order-only traversal. These are added or replaced results; the revised curves do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Theorem A.1 aligns its zero-order-edge assumption with the existing main theorem and adds a covering argument bounding the required degree. Its complexity bound changes the covering radius from tau_M/80 to tau_M/160. Appendix D also replaces the SVD-based derivation with centered second-moment reasoning. The principal denoising rate and phase-analysis results remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: learning a manifold optimizer from noisy samples, combining first- and zero-order traversal, and obtaining favorable denoising–complexity tradeoffs. The conclusion retains the qualification that theoretical guarantees assume an ideal learned graph.

C2.justification: Appendix G adds substantive qualifications: tested autoencoders can achieve higher accuracy, image outputs exhibit pixelation and color artifacts, and radius tuning may extend the method's accuracy range. The new ablation also supports the proposed division of roles between first- and zero-order steps. Existing limitations concerning guarantees for learned landmarks remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, explicit streaming-average and affine-projection formulas in Appendix E, autoencoder architectures and Adam learning rate, and image preprocessing details. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Some ambiguity remains: G.1 describes a two-dimensional bottleneck, whereas Table 2 includes wider bottlenecks; code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gong et al. (2010) and extends the nearest-neighbor efficiency critique to empirical manifold-denoising methods. It also adds the DIV2K dataset reference, Agustsson and Timofte (2017). The broader positioning relative to manifold estimation, Riemannian optimization, and graph search is retained.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains intact, with mostly local condensation, terminology and notation edits, and revised explanations. Appendix D's exposition is reworked and Appendix E collects additional algorithm explanations. Author information, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 adds waveform, autoencoder, image-denoising, and ablation displays in Figures 10 and 13–18, plus an architecture table. Figures 8–9 are redrawn with revised sizing, axes, and legends. The original numerical results table is removed; the original hyperparameter table becomes Table 1, and the retained torus and sphere figures become Figures 11–12.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency argument: v1 compared chiefly against nearest-neighbor search, while v2 adds learned baselines and an ablation directly testing the mixed-order design. The added covering argument strengthens justification of the complexity bound, and implementation documentation improves. Removing the exact results table reduces auditability, and the new image evaluations and autoencoder specifications remain limited, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in supporting evidence and technical clarity.
